chunk_findings.detail: `str.isdigit()` is True for characters that carry the Unicode "digit" property but are *not* decimal digits, and `int()` rejects them. With `--finding ²` (U+00B2, likewise `³`, `¹`, `₂`…), `text.isdigit()` returns True, so evaluation proceeds to `int(text)`, which raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '²'`. Since the whole point of this change is that `--finding` now flows through as a raw string (argparse can no longer reject non-integers), this input reaches `resolve` and produces an unhandled traceback instead of the intended `bad(why, ...)` message the function is written to return. The same predicate is used again at the bottom (`if text.isdigit(): return 0, f"no finding #{text}..."`), which is harmless only because it never calls `int()`. Using an ASCII/decimal check (`text.isascii() and text.isdigit()`, or `text.isdecimal()` plus an ASCII guard) would keep the graceful error path.

chunk_findings.detail: The surface now forwards `a.get("finding")` verbatim (`finding=a.get("finding") or 0`) and both `Param("finding", …)` declarations drop their type, so the entire number-vs-digest decision is delegated to the triage resolver — but numbers and digests share one string space: digests are hex, so a 6+ character digest prefix made only of decimal digits is *also* a syntactically valid finding number. The new regression test only ever feeds prefixes that contain an `f` (`"2f40"`, `"ffffff"`), so the overlap is never exercised, and nothing in the change detects or diagnoses it. Concretely: if `review show` lists `digest 12345678…` and the user copies the 8-char prefix as the help text invites ("a unique digest prefix (6+ hex)"), the token is all-decimal and the resolver's digit branch (which must stay first for `--finding 2` to keep working, since the tests pin `"2f40"` → "at least 6" and `"ffffff"` → digest-listing) parses it as finding #12345678 and fails with a "no such finding/#N" error, instead of resolving the digest the user just copied — exactly the failure mode B8b2e487a13 is supposed to remove. Roughly 2–6% of printed 6–8 char prefixes are all digits, so this is not a corner case the user can avoid by accident; the fix should either accept the digest when it matches (with number fallback) or say unambiguously which form was understood.

chunk_findings.detail: `str.isdigit()` is True for characters whose Unicode numeric type is "Digit" but not "Decimal" — e.g. `'²'`, `'³'`, `'¹'`. `int()` only accepts Decimal digits, so the guard's short-circuit still reaches `int(text)` and raises an unhandled `ValueError`. Concretely: `ddflow review triage X --gate g --finding '²'` (or any caller/regression test that invokes `resolve('²', found, where)` directly, which is the natural way the new helper will be unit-tested) does not return the friendly `(0, why)` tuple the function is documented to return; it propagates `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '²'` out of `resolve` and out of `review.triage`. The line should use `text.isdecimal()` (or catch the conversion), since that is exactly the set of strings `int()` will accept. Note that the later `if text.isdigit():` branch at the bottom is harmless because it never calls `int()`; only line 34 converts.

chunk_findings.detail: `fix_task_holder=holder` is added to the `O.ok("bug.invalid", ...)` return, but `holder` is assigned only inside the block that is guarded by the fix-task condition (the block at lines 245–250, which is indented one level deeper than the return and whose sibling `removed, kept` are the reason the pre-existing code initialises `removed`/`kept` to `""` — the pre-existing doc comment right below states kept is `""` "when the bug has no fix task"). The new variable was not added to that initialisation or to an `else` branch, so on the path where the block is skipped — i.e. any `ddflow bug invalid <id> --reason ...` where the bug record has no `fix_task` (or where the guard is otherwise false) — `removed`/`kept` are `""` as before but `holder` has never been bound. Building the response then raises `UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'holder' where it is not associated with a value`, turning a previously successful no-op invalidation into a crash. Repro: pick a bug with an empty `fix_task`, run `ddflow bug invalid <id> --reason "not a bug"`; the function reaches the new `fix_task_holder=holder` field and dies. Fix: initialise `holder = ""` alongside the `removed`/`kept` defaults (outside the guarded block).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_close.py:250 (`holder` in `bug_invalid`) / return at ~line 270

chunk_findings.detail:
The change rewrites the state guard as `if t.state != OPEN and not mine: return "", "finished"`, i.e. it removes the state check entirely whenever the caller's identity matches the lease holder. Read together with the surrounding code, that guard was the only thing standing between this function and tasks that are already terminal: `t.removed` only catches `task.removed`, and the lease check now only catches *other* holders. Note also that the scenario this change is meant to fix is a task that is still *in* the queue — the old message was "fix task stays in the queue: somebody holds it", so the item was `OPEN`, and the `not mine` on the state guard is not needed for it at all. Its only reachable effect is on non-`OPEN` (terminal) items.

Concrete input: a fix task that reached `FINISHED` (`ddflow complete fix-X ...`) while its lease record still names the caller — e.g. the completing run died after appending `item.finished` but before releasing the lease, or a lease that outlives completion. The caller then runs `ddflow bug invalid <bug>`. `mine` is true, so the `FINISHED` guard is skipped; the code appends `item.abandoned`, calls `L.release` on a finished task, `_ended_by_abandon` sees a non-`OPEN` item and the API reports `fix_task_abandoned=<id>` and runs `CL.dispose_finished` on that item's worktree, so a completed task's record is rewritten as abandoned and its worktree is taken away. (If `fold` instead refuses the `FINISHED -> ABANDONED` transition under `strict=False`, the outcome is different but equally wrong: the lease is released out from under a completed task and `fix_task_removed` is reported non-empty for something that was never `task.removed`.) The only non-`OPEN` state this branch legitimately needs to admit is the claimed/running one the comment names ("a claimed task is RUNNING"); `FINISHED` should still fall through to `"finished"` and be reported as kept.
